probe: M022 T001 — __ngContext__ and window.ng on the fixture, in a development build and a production build

growth.cause: spikes/ng222-app/src/app/trust-bypass-page.ts — the fixture page T001 added (commit 3dfce5c) and T004 extended (commit 68abbb2), routed at /trust-bypass. The growth is that page's emitted code, a real change in both bundles, not measurement noise; both builds are therefore re-recorded rather than the development byte bound widened.
growth.tolerance: the development byte tolerance stays 2000 bytes (DEV_BYTES_TOLERANCE in scripts/ng-context-dev-build.test.mjs); it was not widened to cover this change

packageBuild.why: the development configuration carries a fileReplacement to src/app/app.config.dev.ts, which imports ai-devtools-companion, so the development build resolves the package's exported dist; the production configuration loads no package and does not need it.

differential.meaning: attachPatchData writes __ngContext__ in both configurations — the development bundle names the property through MONKEY_PATCH_KEY_NAME, the production bundle through the minified alias dg — while the surface that would read it, window.ng, is published only in the development build. The property is not dev-only; the debug API is.

served.instanceNote: the instance loads this checkout's extension; the extension's panel is not built by this task, no reading below depends on it, and the probe reads the page realm directly through CDP.
served.how: two static servers over the two emitted browser outputs, read in the page's main world in one new tab that the control-ai-browsers run command closes afterwards; the probe navigates to the development output, reads, then navigates to the production output and reads the same selectors, so the only variable between the two readings is the configuration.
served.note: the development build renames the fixture's App class to _App (Angular's dev-mode class alias), which is why the development reading names it and why the name itself is not the measurement; the production page publishes no window.ng, so no component name is readable there and the reading is null.

ruling.supersededBecause: the production build writes __ngContext__ — measured in the emitted bundle and on the served production page, where app-counter's button carries a numeric __ngContext__ — so a pick on a production page is not a pick without a context.
ruling.statement: __ngContext__ is written in production builds too, so a picked element on a production page carries an Angular context; what a production page lacks is the debug API — window.ng, and with it getOwningComponent and getComponent — that the page realm would use to read that context. The named outcome for a pick the tool cannot resolve on a production page is therefore no-dev-api, not no-dev-context, and the two outcomes must stay distinct: a development page whose element genuinely carries no context can still answer no-dev-context.
ruling.descriptorConsequence: the page realm resolves a picked element through window.ng when the page publishes it, and reports the named outcome no-dev-api when it does not; __ngContext__ itself never crosses the JSON boundary (N2), so its presence is a fact the page realm reads, not a field the descriptor carries.

doesNotSettle.question: does an element that sits inside a component's template — not a component host — carry a dev context that no bundle search can see?
doesNotSettle.settledFor: the fixture's own app-counter button, read on both served pages: hasNgContext true with a numeric context in development and in production (served.reading.development.templateElement, served.reading.production.templateElement).
doesNotSettle.stillOpen: one rendered sample on one fixture is not a per-element guarantee: an element Angular creates after the probe's snapshot (an @if branch that is still false, a @for item added later, a node a directive inserts) and every element of every other app were not read, and a bundle search can see neither.
doesNotSettle.probeThatWouldSettleIt: extend spikes/probes/ng-context.js with a second read after the page mutates a view — click app-counter's Increment, then re-read the same selector and a node an @if branch adds — and re-run it against both static outputs; the same read against another app settles it there.

doesNotSettle.question: does an app built with another Angular version, another optimizer setting or another builder write the property and the surface the same way?
doesNotSettle.settledFor: Angular 22.2.2 as spikes/ng222-app installs it, with the fixture's frozen development and production configurations (pinned in scripts/ng-context-dev-build.test.mjs).
doesNotSettle.stillOpen: the two bundles above are two samples: a different Angular patch level or a bundle optimizer that folds the constant differently can move a marker without moving the behavior, so the markers are a description of these bytes, not of Angular as a whole.
doesNotSettle.probeThatWouldSettleIt: re-run scripts/ng-context-dev-build.test.mjs after the Angular upgrade reads the new bytes, and spikes/probes/ng-context.js on the served output answers the runtime question for the same pair.

reconciliation.note: A clean build (output directory deleted first) emits the same three development bundles as companion-dev-build; T004's three bundles are genuine, not leftovers from a reused output directory.

verdict: measured: both configurations write __ngContext__, and only the development build publishes window.ng; a production page therefore answers no-dev-api, not no-dev-context
